The width of the confidence intervals directly reflects the increasing uncertainty associated with longer time horizons. This broader range accounts for the accumulation of daily and weekly uncertainties, as well as the potential impact of broader economic indicators, policy changes, or shifts in underlying market conditions that become more influential over a longer period.

While the 90% confidence intervals capture a wide range of probable outcomes, there are always unforeseen risks and events that could push the actual results outside these bounds. On the downside, a sudden and severe economic downturn, an unexpected geopolitical crisis, significant negative regulatory changes, or a major industry-specific disruption could cause the value to fall below the lower end of the interval. Conversely, a breakthrough innovation, surprisingly strong economic growth figures, a major positive policy announcement, or an unforeseen surge in demand could lead to outcomes significantly exceeding the upper bound of the forecast, driving the value higher than anticipated. These are typically events that are difficult to predict or quantify in advance, representing tail risks.
